query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A new predictive approach that separately models lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr—by combining state‐of‐the‐art DFT for electronic structure, Boltzmann transport for carrier dynamics, and Green–Kubo simulations using on‐the‐fly ML-trained force fields for phonon scattering—will yield a more accurate prediction of the intrinsic lattice thermal conductivity. Specifically, when applied to low-oxygen (<0.2 wt%) single-phase HfNbTaTiZr, it will predict a lattice conductivity that is approximately 15–30% lower than estimates from earlier methods that conflated both contributions, while also capturing the distinct temperature dependence (e.g., non‐monotonic behavior below 200 K) observed in experiments.
generation.material_initial_state: Defect-free, single-phase random solid solution HfNbTaTiZr prepared (e.g., by spark plasma sintering) with minimized oxygen contamination (<0.2 wt%).
generation.intervention: Application of a new simulation workflow that decouples lattice and electronic heat transport by using DFT for accurate band and force constant calculations, Boltzmann transport for electronic properties, plus Green–Kubo theory driven by on‐the‐fly ML force field training to capture detailed lattice dynamics.
generation.conditions: Valid for temperatures in the range 300–1200 K for low-oxygen samples; predictions regarding non-monotonic temperature dependence below 200 K can be compared with separate low-temperature experiments.
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic-scale force constant fluctuations and lattice distortions captured by ML-trained force fields, which mediate phonon scattering independent of electronic contributions.
generation.mechanism: Accurate DFT-derived band structures and interatomic force constants feed into separate transport formalisms: Boltzmann transport (using relaxation time approximations) for the electronic part and Green–Kubo for lattice dynamics. The ML-trained force fields enhance the resolution of phonon scattering mechanisms due to atomic-scale disorder, thereby decoupling and quantifying the lattice contribution without interference from electronic conduction.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will predict lattice thermal conductivity values that are roughly 15–30% lower than those estimated by earlier conflated models. At around 300 K, the lattice conductivity should be below 1 W/(K m) (in agreement with low-conductivity HEA analogs), and distinct temperature-dependent trends, including potential non-monotonic behavior below 200 K, will be resolved.
generation.baseline: Prior approaches that merge lattice and electronic contributions tend to overestimate the lattice thermal conductivity due to an inability to isolate phonon scattering dynamics in the disordered HEA environment.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to highly purified HfNbTaTiZr samples with negligible oxygen contamination and minimal extrinsic defects. Its predictions may not hold for samples with higher oxygen levels (e.g., ~1 wt%) or significant grain boundary effects.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvement (15–30% reduction) and intricate temperature-dependent trends are subject to uncertainties related to DFT functional choices, ML force field training accuracy, and the extent to which experimental conditions can be replicated in simulations. Behavior below 200 K requires careful experimental validation due to competing scattering mechanisms.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare high-purity HfNbTaTiZr samples with controlled low oxygen levels (<0.2 wt%) and measure thermal conductivities from 100 K to 1200 K. Use time-domain thermoreflectance (or a similar method) to independently extract lattice thermal conductivity from total conductivity, while electrical contributions are separately measured via electronic transport experiments. Compare these measurements with predictions from the new simulation framework.
measurements: Lattice thermal conductivity (e.g., using HFACF analysis from MD experiments and direct thermal measurements)
Electronic thermal conductivity (via independent electrical conductivity and Seebeck coefficient measurements)
Total thermal conductivity across the temperature range
Oxygen content and microstructural purity via chemical and microscale characterization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If experimental measurements of lattice thermal conductivity do not show an approximate 15–30% reduction relative to previous conflated-model predictions, or if the predicted temperature-dependent features (such as non-monotonic behavior below 200 K and sub-1 W/(K m) values at 300 K) are not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: HfNbTaTiZr high entropy alloy was produced by various methods of powder metallurgy including mechanical alloying, sintering, hot isostatic pressing, spark plasma sintering, and high pressure torsion. The microstructure and mechanical properties of HfNbTaTiZr prepared by various methods were examined. It was found that the main problem in fabrication of HfNbTaTiZr alloy by powder metallurgy is oxygen contamination. Samples prepared by cold isostatic pressing followed by sintering and/or hot isostatic pressing contained oxygen in the concentration range of 0.55 wt %–0.85 wt %. Oxygen contamination of samples prepared by mechanical alloying was even higher, and the oxygen concentration in these samples exceeded 1 wt %. Oxygen incorporated into the HfNbTaTiZr samples caused deterioration of mechanical properties (embrittlement) and prevented formation of a single phase random solid solution. Investigations performed in the present work showed that the most promising powder metallurgy method of production of HfNbTaTiZr alloy was spark plasma sintering of gas atomized powder. As mentioned in the introduction, it is worth comparing the vibrational dynamics of our HEA to glasses and to crystalline materials with very large unit cells (CMAs), to identify similarities and differences and establish the place of HEAs with respect to these classes of materials. Specifically, as previously said, the low and weakly temperature dependent thermal conductivity in glasses has been associated to the existence of a strong phonon scattering due to the intrinsic disorder. Such regime, characterized by ΓFWHM ∝ (ℏω)4, has been reported in some glasses at energies corresponding to the deviation of the GVDOS from the Debye behavior and has lately been ascribed mostly to the force-constant disorder at a nanometric lengthscale. Interestingly, the same phenomenology arises in random matrix approaches, which model the vibrational properties of a glass through a random network of force-constants over a regular lattice, quite similarly to the case of our HEA,. It is thus important to check weather the same behavior can be found in our HEA, where force-constant fluctuations are the dominant phonon scattering source.

Based on the heat flux calculated by the MLFF, the heat-flux autocorrelation function (HFACF) of PbSnTeSe was obtained. Figure 8a shows the calculated normalized averaged HFACF at the temperature of 300 K as a function of correlation time. At the beginning, the HFACF starts at one and rapidly drops to oscillate around zero. As correlation time increases, the oscillation gradually decreases, and finally approaches zero, indicating that the HFACF has converged. The HFACF is then used to determine the thermal conductivity (κL) of PbSnTeSe. Figure 8b shows the calculated κL at the temperature of 300 K as a function of correlation time. The trend of κL over correlation time is the same as that of HFACF. Initially, the oscillation is relatively large and finally tends to stabilize converging towards a constant value, hence asserting the proper convergence of our simulations.
